Kim / Marcus — quick technical notes ahead of the deep-dive. I'll prepare slides for the architecture section. High-level answers to the asks below:

- Token budgets / hard cutoffs: Redwood supports token-based quotas at the tenant level. We enforce these via the routing layer (request rejected with 429 or auto-failover to cheaper model variant depending on policy). We support both "soft" alerts and hard cutoffs. Enforcement can be per-minute, per-hour, or monthly.

- Per-customer routing & tiering: We have a routing policy engine that tags incoming requests (customer_id, route_hint) and matches them to deployment pools. Pools can be: dedicated reserved GPU pools (yielding predictable latency), shared cost-optimized pools, or burst pools. Policies can include priority, model whitelist, and fallback variants.

- KV cache isolation: Default mode is shared cache for cost efficiency. We offer two options for stronger isolation: 1) cache partitioning (logical namespace) with quota limits and eviction policies, or 2) fully pinned caches per-tenant which give stronger isolation at the cost of memory overhead and lower overall cache hit-efficiency. For the pilot (top 10 customers) I recommend dedicated pinned caches or dedicated pools depending on latency requirements.

- Auditability / logs: We stream per-request telemetry to your chosen sink (S3/BigQuery) and provide per-tenant usage exports. Token accounting and model/version attribution are included.

Caveats / tradeoffs to call out during the deep-dive:
- Pinned caches increase memory footprint; if many top-tier tenants (>20) we recommend reserved pools rather than pinned caches for cost reasons.
- Hard cutoffs can lead to UX disruption; we typically recommend a staged approach (soft alerts -> throttles -> hard cut).

I'll attach a short slide for costs comparing dedicated pools vs shared slices; Marcus, can you add the expected delta % for 8 / 12 customer pilots?
